The car is at the garage, so I came by bus.
Houses with a garage sell for noticeably more in areas where parking is scarce.

confusables.difference: A garage belongs to one house or one business; a car park is a public space with many bays. You park in a car park, not in a garage, when you go shopping.

entry_json.definition: to come together in a group, or to bring things or information together from different places

example_sentences: Researchers gathered data from more than two thousand households.

contexts.text: Researchers gathered data from more than two thousand households.
We usually gather at my grandmother's house on Sundays.
Governments need to gather reliable evidence before changing the law.

confusables.difference: Collect suggests picking things up one by one on purpose, often as a hobby or a duty: collect stamps, collect the rubbish. Gather suggests bringing scattered things or people together into one place.

entry_json.avoid: 'Gather' meaning 'understand' ('I gather you're leaving') is fine in speech but too casual for Task 2.

entry_json.definition: in most cases, or when you consider something as a whole rather than in detail

example_sentences: Public transport here is generally reliable, though it suffers in winter.
The report is generally positive about the scheme, but it warns about the cost.

contexts.text: Generally speaking, I prefer studying in the morning.
It is generally accepted that early exposure to a second language helps pronunciation.
Rents in the suburbs are generally lower than in the centre.

confusables.difference: Usually is about how often something happens in time. Generally is about how widely something is true across cases. 'I usually walk to work' (frequency); 'walking is generally cheaper' (in most cases).

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in generally'. It is either 'generally' or 'in general'.

entry_json.definition: to produce something such as power, money, work or interest
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wind farms now generate about a quarter of the country's electricity.

The advertisement generated far more interest than the company expected.

contexts.text: Wind farms now generate about a quarter of the country's electricity.
Tourism generates thousands of jobs in my home town.
The scheme is expected to generate enough revenue to pay for itself within a decade.

confusables.difference: Produce is the everyday word and works for physical goods: the factory produces cars. Generate is preferred for power, money, employment and abstract things such as interest or debate.
Create suggests bringing something new into existence, often creative or deliberate. Generate suggests a process that yields an output as a by-product.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'generate a baby' or 'generate a painting'. Generate takes energy, money, data, jobs, interest, not people or artworks.

entry_json.definition: all the people born at about the same time, or the roughly thirty years between a parent's birth and a child's

Three generations of the same family still live in that house.

contexts.text: My grandparents' generation had no expectation of going to university.
We have a duty to leave future generations a habitable planet.
The survey compares attitudes to work across three generations.

confusables.difference: An age group is a band defined by numbers, such as 18 to 24. A generation is defined by shared experience and history, and is much wider.

entry_json.avoid: 'Generation' is a countable noun: say 'the older generation' or 'older generations', never 'the older generation people'.

entry_json.definition: willing to give more money, time or help than is usual or expected; also, larger than expected in amount

It was generous of the neighbours to take our parcels in all summer.

The scholarship is generous enough to cover both fees and living costs.
Countries with generous parental leave tend to have higher birth rates.

confusables.difference: Kind is about warmth and consideration in general. Generous is specifically about giving: money, time, help or space.
A wealthy person has a lot; a generous person gives a lot. The two are not the same, and confusing them makes a sentence say something odd.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'generous with' (time, money) or 'generous to' (a person), not 'generous for'.

entry_json.definition: a style or type of art, writing, film or music with its own recognisable features
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Science fiction is the one genre I never get tired of.
example_sentences: Documentaries have become a far more popular genre since streaming arrived.
The novel deliberately mixes two genres, crime and romance.

contexts.text: Science fiction is the one genre I never get tired of.
The essay examines how each genre shapes what readers expect.
Streaming services have made minority genres commercially viable.

confusables.difference: Style is how one artist or writer does things, and is personal. Genre is a category shared by many works, such as horror or jazz.
Type is the general everyday word. Genre applies only to art, writing, film and music, so it sounds precise there and wrong anywhere else.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'genre' for kinds of food, jobs or transport. Use 'type' or 'kind' for those.

entry_json.definition: kind and careful in the way you treat people or things; not strong, sudden or steep

The path climbs at a gentle slope, so almost anyone can walk it.

contexts.text: My first teacher had a very gentle manner, which helped because I was shy.
Doctors often recommend gentle exercise such as swimming for older patients.
The graph rises at a gentle rate until 2010 and then climbs sharply.

confusables.difference: Soft describes what something feels like to touch. Gentle describes how someone or something acts: a soft pillow, but a gentle push.
Polite is about following social rules. Gentle is about not using force or harshness, and is warmer.

entry_json.avoid: 'Gentle' is not the adverb. Use 'gently': 'she closed the door gently', not 'gentle'.

entry_json.definition: a polite word for a man, used especially when speaking to or about someone respectfully; also a man who behaves honourably
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The gentleman at the desk explained the whole procedure very patiently.

He was enough of a gentleman to admit that the mistake was his.

contexts.text: The gentleman at the desk explained the whole procedure very patiently.
Ladies and gentlemen, thank you all for coming this evening.
Please could you show this gentleman to the waiting room.

confusables.difference: Man is neutral and always safe. Gentleman adds politeness or distance, and can sound old-fashioned if used of a friend.
Written as two words this means a man who is gentle, which is a different thing entirely. Keep it as one word.

entry_json.avoid: The plural is 'gentlemen', not 'gentlemans'. Avoid it in Task 2 essays; 'men' is the neutral choice there.

entry_json.definition: the spirit of a dead person that some people believe can be seen or felt
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I don't believe in ghosts, but I still wouldn't sleep in that house.

Ghost stories are a big part of the folklore where I come from.

contexts.text: I don't believe in ghosts, but I still wouldn't sleep in that house.
Every region has its own ghost stories, and they say a lot about local history.
After the mine closed, the village became something of a ghost town.

confusables.difference: Spirit is broader and can be positive or religious. Ghost is specifically the frightening image of a dead person.

entry_json.avoid: Keep ghosts out of Task 2 unless the question is about beliefs or traditions; they read as off-topic.

entry_json.definition: extremely large, much bigger than other things of the same kind
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A giant screen had been set up in the square so everyone could watch.
example_sentences: Giant supermarkets on the edge of town have emptied the high street.
The museum's giant model of the solar system takes up a whole hall.

contexts.text: A giant screen had been set up in the square so everyone could watch.
Giant retailers can afford to sell below cost until small shops close.
There was a giant queue outside the exam hall.

confusables.difference: Huge is the safer written choice and simply means very big. Giant is more visual and slightly informal, and suits objects you can picture.
Enormous is neutral in register and fine in an essay. Giant used before a noun can sound like advertising language.

entry_json.avoid: In formal writing prefer 'enormous', 'vast' or 'substantial'; 'giant' reads as conversational.

entry_json.definition: pleased and happy about something, usually about a particular event or piece of news
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I'm glad I chose the evening course, because the mornings were impossible.
example_sentences: She was glad to hear that her application had finally been accepted.
I'd be glad to help you practise before the speaking test.

contexts.text: I'm glad I chose the evening course, because the mornings were impossible.
I'd be glad to show you around if you ever visit.
We were all glad when the exams were finally over.

confusables.difference: Happy can describe a lasting state ('a happy childhood'); glad almost always reacts to one specific thing and cannot go before a noun.
Pleased is slightly more formal and often about satisfaction with a result. Glad is warmer and more personal.

entry_json.avoid: You cannot put 'glad' before a noun. Say 'a happy day', never 'a glad day'.

entry_json.definition: affecting or including the whole world
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Climate change is a global problem that no single country can solve alone.

English has become the global language of academic publishing.

contexts.text: Climate change is a global problem that no single country can solve alone.
Working for a global company means answering emails at strange hours.
The chart compares global energy consumption in 1990 and 2020.

confusables.difference: International means between countries and implies borders being crossed. Global means the whole planet taken as one unit.
Worldwide is usually about reach or spread ('sold worldwide'). Global is more often used of systems, problems and markets.

entry_json.avoid: 'Global' has no plural and is not a noun. Write 'global issues', not 'the globals'.

entry_json.definition: a piece of clothing that covers the hand, with a separate part for each finger
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I never leave home in January without a pair of gloves.

contexts.text: I never leave home in January without a pair of gloves.
Staff are required to wear disposable gloves when handling food.
I lost one glove on the bus, which is somehow worse than losing both.

confusables.difference: A mitten keeps all four fingers together in one pocket; a glove has a separate sleeve for each finger.

entry_json.avoid: Gloves come in pairs: say 'a pair of gloves', not 'a gloves'.

entry_json.definition: things that are produced to be sold; products moved or traded, rather than services
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap imported goods have made it hard for local workshops to survive.
example_sentences: The port handles millions of tonnes of goods every year.
Electronic goods are the country's largest single export.

contexts.text: Cheap imported goods have made it hard for local workshops to survive.
The chart shows the value of goods exported between 2000 and 2015.
Deliveries of household goods have got much faster where I live.

confusables.difference: Products is the ordinary word for what a company makes and can be singular. Goods is always plural and belongs to trade, transport and economics.
Goods are things you can touch; services are work done for you. Essays about economies usually need both words, correctly separated.

entry_json.avoid: 'Goods' takes a plural verb and has no singular: 'the goods were delivered', never 'a good was delivered'.

entry_json.definition: to control and legally run a country or region; also, to control how something works or happens
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The party has governed the country for almost twenty years.
example_sentences: Strict rules govern how personal data may be stored and shared.

contexts.text: The party has governed the country for almost twenty years.
Strict rules govern how personal data may be stored and shared.
I think local councils should govern local matters, not central government.

confusables.difference: Rule suggests power held by one person or a small group, often without consent. Govern is neutral and suggests administration under law.
You manage a company, a team or your time. You govern a country or a set of processes. Swapping them sounds wrong in both directions.

entry_json.avoid: 'Govern' is a verb; the noun is 'government'. Write 'the government decided', not 'the govern decided'.

entry_json.definition: to take hold of something suddenly and roughly; informally, to get something quickly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He grabbed his coat and ran for the last train.

contexts.text: He grabbed his coat and ran for the last train.
Shall we grab something to eat before the film?
A headline has about two seconds to grab a reader's attention.

confusables.difference: Take is neutral. Grab adds speed and force, and often a hint of rudeness or urgency.
You catch something moving through the air; you grab something that is still. 'Catch the ball', 'grab the rail'.

entry_json.avoid: 'Grab a coffee' and 'grab a seat' are conversational. Do not use 'grab' in Task 2 writing.

entry_json.definition: a mark showing the quality of a student's work, or a level in a scale of quality or rank
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I needed a good grade in maths to get onto the engineering course.

contexts.text: I needed a good grade in maths to get onto the engineering course.
Employers increasingly look beyond grades to what candidates can actually do.
Students are placed in classes according to the grade they achieved in the entrance test.

confusables.difference: In British English a mark is the number of points you score; a grade is the letter or band that number falls into. 62 marks might be a grade B.
A score is a raw result, common in tests and sport. A grade interprets that result on a scale.

entry_json.avoid: In British English 'grade' is not a school year. Say 'Year 9' or 'the third year', not 'grade nine', unless describing an American system.

entry_json.definition: slowly, over a long period of time, in small stages rather than all at once
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city gradually replaced its diesel buses with electric ones.
example_sentences: Her confidence in speaking improved gradually over the whole year.
Unemployment fell gradually between 2012 and 2019.

contexts.text: Unemployment fell gradually between 2012 and 2019.
My listening got better gradually rather than all at once.
Attitudes to recycling have gradually shifted over the past two decades.

confusables.difference: Slowly is about low speed at any moment. Gradually is about change happening in stages over time. A car moves slowly; prices rise gradually.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 pair 'gradually' with a verb of change ('rose gradually'), not with a state verb ('was gradually high').

The chart shows grain production in four countries over thirty years.
We grew up on a farm, so the smell of grain still reminds me of home.

confusables.difference: Cereal is the technical term for the plants themselves (wheat, oats, maize). Grain is the harvested seed and the traded commodity.
A seed is what you plant to grow a new plant. Grain is what you harvest to eat or sell.

entry_json.avoid: As a crop, 'grain' is uncountable: 'we export grain', not 'we export grains'. Only individual pieces are countable.

entry_json.definition: impressive in size or appearance, often in a way that suggests wealth or importance

The wedding was held in a really grand old hotel.
The project was conceived on a grand scale but delivered in pieces.

confusables.difference: Great is about quality or degree and is far more common. Grand is about scale and splendour, and is mainly visual.
Luxurious means expensive and comfortable to use. Grand means impressive to look at, which is not the same thing.

entry_json.avoid: 'Grand' is not a synonym for 'very good'. 'A grand idea' sounds dated or ironic in British English.

entry_json.definition: a sum of money given by a government or organisation for a particular purpose, which does not have to be repaid
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A small research grant paid for the equipment we needed.
example_sentences: Students from low-income families can apply for a maintenance grant.
The council awarded a grant to restore the market hall.

contexts.text: Students from low-income families can apply for a maintenance grant.
I only managed to study abroad because I got a grant.
Public grants for renewable energy have risen sharply since 2010.

A scholarship is usually awarded for merit and covers study. A grant can be for study, research, building work or business, and is often need-based.

entry_json.avoid: The verb 'grant' means 'to allow or give formally' ('the visa was granted'). Do not write 'the government granted a grant'.

entry_json.definition: feeling or showing thanks to someone for something they have done for you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I'm grateful to my parents for never pushing me towards a particular career.
example_sentences: We are extremely grateful for all the help the volunteers gave.

contexts.text: I'm grateful to my parents for never pushing me towards a particular career.
I would be grateful if you could send the documents before the deadline.
Patients were grateful for the extra time the nurses gave them.

confusables.difference: Thankful is usually about relief that something bad did not happen ('thankful nobody was hurt'). Grateful is about appreciating what someone did for you.
Appreciative is more formal and often about recognising quality. Grateful is about owing thanks.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is 'grateful to a person for a thing'. Do not write 'grateful of'.

entry_json.definition: an increase in size, amount or importance; the process of developing

There has been enormous growth in the number of people working from home.
The growth of my home town over ten years has been hard to keep up with.

confusables.difference: Increase is a plain rise in a number and is fully countable ('a sharp increase'). Growth suggests development over time and is usually uncountable.
Development is about becoming more advanced or complete. Growth is about becoming bigger. An economy can grow without developing.

entry_json.avoid: 'Growth' is normally uncountable: write 'rapid growth', not 'a rapid growths'.

entry_json.definition: to promise firmly that something will happen or is certainly true, or to promise to repair or replace a product
entry_json.own_context_sentence: No course can guarantee a particular band score, whatever the advertising says.

Higher pay does not guarantee that staff will stay.

contexts.text: No course can guarantee a particular band score, whatever the advertising says.
The laptop is guaranteed for three years against manufacturing faults.
I can't guarantee I'll be free, but I'll try to come.

confusables.difference: A promise is personal and can be broken without consequence. A guarantee is formal and usually carries a remedy if it fails.
Ensure means to make sure something happens by taking action. Guarantee is a statement of certainty to someone else, often backed by a commitment.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to protect a place, people or property, or to stop prisoners escaping

Employing more guards has not reduced theft in the shopping centre.
There was a guard on the platform who told us which carriage to use.

confusables.difference: A guard is employed by a private company or an institution and protects one place. A police officer works for the state and has legal powers.
Guard is the person or the act of watching; protect is the verb for keeping something from harm. 'Guards protect the site', not 'guards guard the site'.

entry_json.avoid: The verb 'guard' takes a direct object: 'guard the entrance', not 'guard for the entrance'.

entry_json.definition: having done something wrong or illegal; also, feeling ashamed because you have done something wrong

I feel guilty every time I take a taxi instead of walking.
Suspects are presumed innocent until proved guilty.

confusables.difference: Responsible states who caused something, with no moral judgement. Guilty says the act was wrong and blames the person for it.
Ashamed is about how others might see you. Guilty is about what your own conscience says.

entry_json.definition: to deal with a situation, person or problem successfully; also to touch or move something with your hands

I'm not great at handling stress, so I try to plan ahead.
Schools need clear procedures for handling bullying.

entry_json.definition: to attach something at the top so that the rest of it is free, or to be attached in that way

contexts.text: We hung the map on the wall above the desk.
A large clock hangs above the entrance to the hall.
I hang my coat by the door so I don't forget it.

confusables.difference: Hold means to keep something in your hand or arms. Hang means to fix it so gravity keeps it in place while nobody touches it.
Attach is neutral about direction; hang always means from above, with the object free below.

entry_json.avoid: The past tense is 'hung' for objects. 'Hanged' is used only for executing a person.

entry_json.definition: the feeling or state of being happy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Studies suggest that beyond a certain income, extra money adds little to happiness.

There is a strong link between close friendships and long-term happiness.

contexts.text: Studies suggest that beyond a certain income, extra money adds little to happiness.
For me happiness is mostly about having enough free time.
Governments have begun to measure national happiness alongside economic output.

confusables.difference: Pleasure is a short, immediate enjoyment from a particular thing. Happiness is a broader and more lasting condition of life.
Satisfaction comes from meeting a need or achieving a goal. Happiness does not need an achievement behind it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Happiness' is uncountable: write 'brings happiness', never 'a happiness' or 'happinesses'.

entry_json.definition: almost not at all; very little
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I hardly used my car last year because everything was within walking distance.
example_sentences: There is hardly any difference between the two courses in practice.
She had hardly finished speaking when the bell went.

contexts.text: I hardly used my car last year because everything was within walking distance.
There is hardly any evidence that longer school days improve results.
I hardly ever watch television now.

confusables.difference: Hard means with effort or difficulty ('she works hard'). Hardly means almost not at all ('she hardly works'). The two say opposite things.
Rarely is about how often something happens. Hardly is about degree or amount, and needs 'ever' to talk about frequency.

entry_json.avoid: 'Hardly' is already negative. Never write 'I don't hardly know'; write 'I hardly know'.

entry_json.definition: damage or injury caused to a person, an animal or the environment
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air pollution does real harm to children's developing lungs.
example_sentences: The policy was intended to help small businesses but did more harm than good.
There is no harm in asking the tutor for extra reading.

contexts.text: Air pollution does real harm to children's developing lungs.
Banning cars from the centre completely might do more harm than good to local shops.
I don't think a bit of screen time does any harm.

confusables.difference: Damage is usually physical and visible, and applies to objects and buildings. Harm is broader and covers health, wellbeing and reputation.
An injury is a specific wound to a body. Harm is the general effect, and can be gradual or invisible.

entry_json.avoid: 'Harm' is uncountable: 'cause harm', not 'cause a harm' or 'harms'.

entry_json.definition: causing damage or injury to health, to the environment or to something's development
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Excessive screen time before bed is harmful to sleep quality.
example_sentences: The factory released harmful chemicals into the river for years.
Constant comparison on social media can be harmful to young people's confidence.

contexts.text: Excessive screen time before bed is harmful to sleep quality.
The factory released harmful chemicals into the river for years.
I think fast food is harmful if you eat it every day, not now and then.

confusables.difference: Dangerous means something could suddenly cause serious injury. Harmful means it does damage, often slowly and invisibly. Smoking is harmful; a cliff edge is dangerous.
The direct opposite. Watch the ending: 'harmless' means it does no damage at all.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'harmful to', not 'harmful for'.

entry_json.definition: the title of a newspaper or news article, printed in large letters above the text
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The headline was far more dramatic than anything in the article itself.
example_sentences: Most readers see only the headline and never open the story.
The scandal made front-page headlines for a week.

contexts.text: The headline was far more dramatic than anything in the article itself.
I usually just scan the headlines on my phone in the morning.
Editors write headlines to attract clicks rather than to summarise fairly.

confusables.difference: A title names a book, film or essay. A headline sits above a news story and is written to catch attention.
A caption explains a photograph or a figure. A headline introduces the whole article.

entry_json.avoid: 'The headlines' can mean the main news items on radio or television, not just printed titles.

entry_json.definition: the ability to hear; also a formal meeting at which evidence is heard and a decision is made
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Years of loud machinery had damaged his hearing.
example_sentences: Loud headphones are a growing cause of hearing loss among young people.
The court hearing lasted three days.

contexts.text: Loud headphones are a growing cause of hearing loss among young people.
My grandfather's hearing isn't what it was, so we all speak up.
The tribunal scheduled a hearing for the following month.

confusables.difference: Hearing is the physical ability of the ears. Listening is paying attention on purpose. You can hear a lecture without listening to it.
Sound is what travels through the air. Hearing is your capacity to receive it.

entry_json.avoid: In the sense of the ability, 'hearing' is uncountable: 'his hearing is poor', not 'his hearings'.

entry_json.definition: the system that keeps a building warm, and the process of doing so
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Older flats here have no central heating at all.
example_sentences: Heating costs rose sharply over the winter.
Better insulation cuts heating bills far more than turning the thermostat down.

contexts.text: Older flats here have no central heating at all.
Heating accounts for the largest share of household energy use.
We only turn the heating on in the evenings to save money.
